definition: Email Service Provider — a platform used to send, manage, and measure marketing or transactional email campaigns.
Click-Through Rate — the percentage of email recipients who clicked one or more links in a message.
The percentage of delivered emails that were opened. Increasingly noisy due to Apple Mail Privacy Protection and similar features.
The ability for legitimate email to reach the inbox rather than spam or promotions folders.
Sender Policy Framework — a DNS record that lists which servers are allowed to send email for a domain.
DomainKeys Identified Mail — a cryptographic signature that proves an email was authorized by the sending domain.
Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance — a policy that tells receivers how to handle SPF/DKIM failures and where to send reports.
Brand Indicators for Message Identification — a standard that can display a brand logo in supporting inboxes when DMARC is enforced.
Gradually increasing send volume from a new domain or IP so mailbox providers learn to trust the sender.
A set of test inboxes across providers used to monitor placement, rendering, and deliverability.
A subscription process where a user confirms their email address before being added to a mailing list.
A subscription process that adds an address immediately after form submission without a confirmation email.
Message triggered by a user action — password resets, receipts, shipping updates — rather than a marketing broadcast.
Automated messages tied to a customer journey stage such as welcome, onboarding, win-back, or renewal.
Splitting an audience into groups based on behavior, attributes, or preferences so messaging can be more relevant.
Adapting content, offers, or send timing to an individual recipient using known data and behavior.
A free resource (ebook, checklist, template) offered in exchange for an email address.
A markup language and framework for building responsive HTML emails with a simplified component syntax.
Amazon Simple Email Service — a cloud email-sending API often used for transactional mail and self-hosted ESPs.
Ongoing cleanup of invalid, inactive, or risky addresses to protect sender reputation and improve engagement.
Comparing two versions of an email (subject line, content, send time) to see which performs better.
The portion of an email visible without scrolling, in the preview pane or on open.
An automated email triggered by a specific action or time delay.
A list of IP addresses or domains flagged as spam sources by mailbox providers or blocklist operators.
The percentage of sent emails that were not delivered to the recipient's inbox.
A sender who dispatches a high volume of email, subject to added authentication requirements from Gmail and Yahoo.
U.S. law setting rules for commercial email, including opt-out requirements and sender identification.
A visual overlay showing where recipients clicked within an email.
The percentage of opened emails that generated at least one click.
An unsolicited email sent to a recipient with no prior relationship, typically for outreach or sales.
The percentage of email recipients who completed a desired action, such as a purchase or signup.
A user-defined data point (e.g., first name, birthday) stored per subscriber and used for personalization.
An IP address used exclusively by one sender, giving them full control over their own sending reputation.
The percentage of sent emails that successfully reach a recipient's inbox without bouncing.
A series of pre-scheduled emails sent automatically over time based on a trigger or schedule.
Email content that changes per recipient based on data, behavior, or segment.
The software or app used to read email, such as Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail.
A measure of how recipients interact with email, including opens, clicks, and replies.
The snippet of text shown after the subject line in an inbox preview.
A system where mailbox providers notify senders when a recipient marks an email as spam.
A permanent delivery failure, often due to an invalid or non-existent email address.
Whether an email lands in the primary inbox versus a spam or promotions folder.
A score mailbox providers assign to a sending IP based on its sending history and behavior.
The rate at which subscribers unsubscribe, bounce, or become inactive over time.
The net rate at which an email list gains new subscribers over a period.
A company that operates email infrastructure for recipients, such as Gmail or Outlook.
Software that triggers and manages email sequences based on subscriber behavior or data.
A recurring email sent to subscribers containing curated content, updates, or news.
A mechanism, required by Gmail and Yahoo for bulk senders, letting recipients unsubscribe in a single action.
Dashboards (e.g., Google Postmaster Tools) that let senders monitor domain reputation and delivery metrics.
A page where subscribers can manage the type and frequency of emails they receive.
A series of emails targeting inactive subscribers to win back their attention or clean the list.
An email designed to render correctly across different screen sizes and devices.
Using data or algorithms to determine the best time to send email to each subscriber.
A score reflecting how trustworthy a sending domain or IP appears to mailbox providers.
A temporary delivery failure, such as a full inbox or a server timeout.
An email address used to identify senders with poor list hygiene, often set up by mailbox providers or blocklists.
The line of text that summarizes an email's content and appears first in an inbox.
An individual who has opted in to receive email from a sender.
A list of email addresses excluded from future sends, such as unsubscribes or bounces.
Deliberately limiting the rate of email sends to protect sender reputation.
Sending an email based on each recipient's local time zone rather than a single send time.
An email automatically sent in response to a specific subscriber action or event.
The percentage of recipients who opt out of a mailing list after receiving a campaign.
Tags appended to links to track campaign performance in analytics tools.
The first automated email sent to a new subscriber after signup.
A list of trusted senders that mailbox providers or filters treat favorably.
An email sequence aimed at re-engaging subscribers who have gone inactive.
A structured data file, sometimes used to power dynamic or catalog-based email content.
Information a customer proactively and intentionally shares with a brand, such as stated preferences.
An automated message reminding a shopper to complete a purchase they left in their cart.
Descriptive text attached to an image that displays when images are blocked or read aloud by screen readers.
A unique credential used to authenticate requests to an email service provider's API.
Technical standards like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC that verify a sender's identity to mailbox providers.
A one-time email sent to an entire list or segment, as opposed to an automated or triggered message.
Grouping subscribers by a shared starting point, such as signup date, to compare their behavior over time.
The percentage of delivered emails that recipients mark as spam or junk.
A message verifying a subscriber's email address or a completed action, such as a signup or purchase.
A stored collection of subscriber email addresses and associated data used for sending campaigns.
Software that tracks customer interactions and data, often integrated with email marketing platforms.
Coordinating messaging across email, SMS, push, and other channels for a consistent customer experience.
Converting stylesheet rules into inline HTML attributes so styles render consistently across email clients.
Email content designed to remain readable and on-brand when viewed in a device's dark color scheme.
Supplementing subscriber records with additional information from third-party or internal sources.
A review of sending practices, authentication, and reputation to diagnose and fix inbox placement issues.
A score mailbox providers assign to a sending domain based on its historical sending behavior.
Adding email addresses to existing customer records using a third-party matching service.
The frequency and timing pattern at which emails are sent to subscribers.
Writing persuasive, concise text for email subject lines, preview text, and body content.
Subscriber disengagement caused by receiving too many emails too often.
A limit on how many emails a subscriber can receive within a given time period.
A server or service that handles the sending and receiving of email between networks.
The metadata portion of an email containing routing, authentication, and sender information.
Paying to send a campaign to a third party's opted-in list, distinct from purchasing addresses outright.
The stages a subscriber moves through, from signup to purchase to retention, driven by email.
How an email's layout, fonts, and images actually display across different clients and devices.
A reusable, pre-designed email layout that can be populated with new content for each send.
Checking that an email address is valid and deliverable before adding it to a list or sending to it.
A composite metric ranking subscribers by how actively they open, click, and interact with email.
A signup form triggered when a visitor's cursor behavior suggests they're about to leave a page.
Information a company collects directly from its own audience, such as purchase or browsing history.
The point a subscriber occupies in a marketing funnel, such as awareness, consideration, or decision.
Gmail's inbox categorization feature that sorts incoming mail into Primary, Promotions, Social, and other tabs.
An email formatted with HTML markup to include styling, images, and layout, as opposed to plain text.
A mail client setting that prevents images from loading automatically until the recipient allows it.
A contact who has not opened or clicked an email within a defined recent period.
Email that supports in-message actions like carousels, forms, or live content without leaving the inbox.
A company providing internet access, sometimes also operating its own mail servers and spam filters.
A mail client folder where suspected spam or unwanted email is automatically routed.
A specific, measurable metric used to evaluate the success of an email program or campaign.
The web page a subscriber arrives at after clicking a link in an email.
A contact who was previously engaged but has stopped opening or clicking over an extended period.
Automatically inserting personalized data, such as a name, into a template to generate individual emails.
A collection of email addresses that have opted in to receive communications from a sender.
A contact whose engagement signals, often including email activity, indicate readiness for further marketing.
A unique identifier assigned to each email, used for tracking and troubleshooting delivery.
Testing multiple email elements at once, such as subject line and image, to see which combination performs best.
A series of emails introducing a new user or customer to a product or service.
The action a recipient takes to stop receiving future email communications.
An approach to marketing that relies on explicit subscriber consent before sending communications.
